name: func_801681A0
notes: Exact boundary from the verified overlay split. Draws the password screen's selection frame around the record pointed to by the first argument into the ordering table in the second. It builds two primitives in the PS1 scratchpad - a five-word three-vertex polyline at 0x1F800000 with code 0x48 and a four-word two-vertex line at 0x1F800040 with code 0x50 - and submits each through func_8005B260 eight times with priority from the record's s16 at +0x14 masked to 16 bits and otag 1. The record's geometry is x at +0x30 y at +0x32 width at +0x3C and height at +0x3E all halfwords. Four submissions draw corner brackets one per corner: the top left runs from x minus 1 and y plus 3 up to x minus 1 and y minus 1 then right to x plus 3; the other three mirror it about x plus width and y plus height. Four more draw lines from the frame out to the screen edges - up from the top centre to y zero down from the bottom centre to y 192 left from the left centre to x zero and right from the right centre to x 320 - which is the callout that ties the frame to whatever is off-screen. Both primitives take colour 0x0000FF00 written as one word at +4 before the length and code bytes overwrite +3 and +7 and the polyline takes a second colour word 0x55555555 at +0x14. Builds 150 instructions against 147. Lever found: the width and height locals must be unsigned. As s32 the halving for the two centre lines emits srav where the target has srlv - GCC cannot prove a value loaded with lhu into a signed local is non-negative. Measured and not helping: a u16 local for the x plus 3 corner value which the target spills with sw and reloads with lhu. What remains is three instructions of register pressure - the target keeps x in a callee-saved register and adds 2 in place for the last line while the build spills the sum through the stack. Reconstructed independently and three findings correct or sharpen the note above. First a semantic correction: the four callout lines are symmetric and all start two pixels inside the frame, so the bottom line begins at y plus height minus 2 rather than minus 1, matching the top at y plus 2, the left at x plus 2 and the right at x plus width minus 2. Second, the priority is not masked in the source at all. Writing pri equals the s16 at plus 0x14 and 0xFFFF folds the lh and the andi into a single lhu, which is why the mask looked like it belonged to the load; the target's lh followed by a distant andi is what a u16 third parameter on func_8005B260 produces, with the conversion done once at the first call site and reused. That alone took the candidate from 124 differing positions to 88. Third, the target updates two values in place rather than recomputing them: x plus equals 2 before the left line, and the bottom local minus equals 2 before the bottom line, where the bottom local already holds y plus height from the third corner. The residual is now exact and is three instructions in one place. The target keeps x in callee-saved s6 and spends one addiu s6 s6 2; the build spills x and spends lw, addiu, sw and lhu. The competing value is the x plus 3 corner, which the target parks in a stack slot with sw and reloads with lhu. Re-measured against this corrected shape and still inert: declaring the x plus 3 local u16 does not make GCC spill it, and spelling x plus 3 inline at both corners does not free the register either because GCC re-forms the common subexpression. So the open question is only which of the two values the allocator spills. Correction to the reading above, which created a false lead. The sw followed by lhu on the spilled x plus 3 corner is not a type tell and does not mean the source declares that value u16. Rebuilding this candidate and looking at its own output shows the identical idiom on the spilled x, which is a plain s32 local: sw to the slot, then lw when the value feeds arithmetic and lhu when it feeds a halfword store. The reload width follows the use, not the declaration, so the pair says nothing about the declared type and only says the value is in a stack slot. Both builds therefore spend the same idiom on whichever value loses the register; the whole residual is which one that is. By use count x should win as it does in the target - it feeds x minus 1, x plus 3, x plus width, the centre sum and x plus 2, five uses against the corner value's two. Measured against this shape and not helping: declaring the corner value u16, re-confirmed; and assigning x plus 2 to a separate local instead of updating x in place, which leaves both the count and the positions unchanged, so the in-place update is not what costs x its register. The residual is not a two-way contest between x and the x plus 3 corner, and reading it that way has been sending attempts at the wrong question. Read off the target directly: it uses all nine callee-saved registers and spills three values to the frame, not one. s0 and s1 hold the two scratchpad primitives, s8 the ordering table, s4 the priority already converted to 16 bits, s5 y, s6 x, s2 the width, s3 y plus height, and s7 x minus 1. The frame holds the height at 16(sp), stored immediately after it is loaded and before any call and reloaded twice, x plus 3 at 20(sp), and x plus width at 24(sp). So the target keeps x and spills three separate values, and the question is not which of two loses a register. Two asymmetries in that assignment are the actual leads. First, x minus 1 has its own callee-saved register: it is computed once at instruction 40 and read at both left corners, 43 and 44 for the top and 82 and 83 for the bottom, so the source names it as a local rather than recomputing it per corner. Any candidate that spells x minus 1 at each corner is competing for a different set of registers than the target and should not be expected to match. Second, the two dimensions are treated oppositely although they are written the same way: the width lives in s2 for the whole function while the height is spilled the moment it is loaded, and correspondingly y plus height keeps s3 while x plus width is spilled. So whatever distinguishes them is between the width and the height, not between x and its corner. Both of those are checkable against a rebuilt candidate and neither has been tried. Rebuilt from the corrected reading and it now builds 148 against 147, one over rather than three, with 139 differing positions. The shape that gets there writes only the fields that change at each submission rather than all six: the first corner sets both x fields to x minus 1, both upper y fields to y minus 1 and the lower to y plus 3 and the third x to x plus 3; the second changes only the three x fields to x plus width plus 1 and x plus width minus 3; the third changes only the three y fields against y plus height; and the fourth changes only the x fields back. The four callouts likewise touch only what moves. Both x and y are updated in place at the end, x plus equals 2 and y plus equals height over two, and the width local is overwritten by x plus width over two, which is why the width can share a register with that centre and the height cannot. The residual reframes again and the new reading is checkable. Side by side the target holds the priority, y, x, x minus 1 and the ordering table in s4 to s8 and spills the height, x plus 3 and x plus width; the candidate holds the priority, y, x plus 3, x minus 1 and the width, and spills x, the height and the ordering table. The candidate never gives the ordering table a register at all: it stores the incoming argument to the frame at instruction 20 and reloads it before every one of the eight calls, where the target copies it to s8 at instruction 3 and never touches memory. That is the root difference rather than the x contest, because a spilled ordering table frees exactly the register that then goes to x plus 3. So the question to answer next is why the second parameter loses its register, not which of x and its corner wins one. Re-measured against this corrected shape: spelling x plus 3 inline at both corners instead of naming it is byte-identical, so the recorded note that the compiler re-forms that common subexpression holds here too and that avenue stays closed. Correction to the previous entry: the spilled ordering table is not what costs the extra instruction. Each reload of it replaces one move from a callee-saved register one for one, eight sites either way, so the spill is count-neutral and only changes which registers hold what. The single extra instruction is x. The target updates it in place with one addiu s6 s6 2 before the left callout, while the candidate has x in a frame slot and spends lw, addiu and sw there. So the whole residual is that one update, and the question is only whether x holds a register at that point. Three things were measured against the rebuilt candidate and none of them moves it. Copying the ordering-table parameter into a local before the first call is coalesced away and gives byte-identical output. Writing the fourth corner's x as x minus 1 plus 4 rather than x plus 3, so that it derives from a value already in a register instead of forming the same common subexpression, is also byte-identical, which strengthens the recorded finding that this expression cannot be kept out of its own register by how it is spelled. Both candidates spill exactly three values, so this is a preference rather than a pressure problem. One further difference is real but count-neutral and worth recording so it is not mistaken for a lead: both halvings in the target are srlv against the register that holds the calls' fourth argument, the constant 1, where the candidate emits an immediate srl. The target is reusing the argument constant as the shift amount, which means that constant is a shared pseudo across the whole function rather than eight separate literals.

name: TextBox_GetGlyphAt
notes: Exact overlay match with gcc_2_8_1_g0_split. Searches the node list at entry+0x24 of the 100-byte record for a node whose x at +0xC and y at +0xE match the arguments; the walk stops when bit 0x80 of the byte at +0x11 is clear and returns the node or zero. Nodes are 0x1C bytes. Three levers: the table base goes in its own local because writing base + index * 100 + 0x24 folds 0x24 into the %lo; the loop is for(;;) with explicit returns because while (flags & 0x80) lets GCC peel the first test and rotate; and the flags exit returns inline rather than breaking to a shared trailing return which costs the exiting branch its delay slot. The induction-variable blocker recorded earlier was a symptom of the rotation rather than a separate problem: the peeled load gave GCC +0x11 to build the combined giv from instead of the target's +0xE and the negative offsets followed from that.

notes: Exact overlay match with gcc_2_8_1_g0_split. A twelve frame squash on the object at +0x4C. name: func_80168AB4
notes: Exact boundary from the verified overlay split. Password widget slide, the same 8.8 fixed point shape as FreeDuel_UpdateCursorTween. Bit 0x80 of the state byte at +0x6C marks the slide already primed: the first pass sets it calls func_800429D8 and divides the distance from the current pair at +0x30 and +0x32 to the target pair at +0x44 and +0x46 shifted left 8 by the frame count at +0x60 into the per-frame steps at +0x36 and +0x38. Bit 0x40 means the widget is retiring - each frame decrements +0x60 and at zero or below releases it through func_8004036C. Otherwise it advances through func_80042A78 and decrements +0x60; while that stays positive it spawns a trail sprite through func_8004002C and func_800400AC with func_80040510 at the widget's current position size 16 by 16 using the bytes at +0x5C +0x5D and +0x66 and the halfwords at +0x40 and +0x42 then sets its colour word to 0x606060 its timer to 6 its hook to func_80042BC0 and or-s 0x50000000 into its flags. At zero it sets bit 0x40 snaps the position pair to the target as one 32-bit word rearms +0x60 to 2 and asks TextBox_GetGlyphAt for node 3 at D_8016D42C shifted left 4; a non-null node is handed to func_80168CDC with 3 and the result gets hook func_801688AC and state 5. Builds 138 of 138 instructions with 10 differing positions under gcc_2_8_1_g0_split. Lever found: the two step results must be stored inline rather than through named locals. With locals GCC folds the two reads of +0x60 into one and the body builds 136; storing +0x36 between the two divisions blocks that common subexpression so the divisor is reloaded and the scheduler then sinks both stores to the end by itself which is what the target shows. Measured and not helping: a struct typed widget instead of byte-pointer casts; a named local for the frame count; the three snap stores written in any of three orders since GCC reorders provably distinct offsets off one base; the node x argument named in a local either before the snap stores or immediately before the call; the shift written as a multiply by 16; and profiles gcc_2_8_1_g0_no_sched2_split gcc_2_8_1_g0_split_no_sched1 and gcc_2_8_1_g8_split which build 139 142 and 137. What remains is one rotation in the snap block: the target opens it with the move of zero into a2 - the third argument for TextBox_GetGlyphAt - and closes it with the store of 2 into +0x60 while the build opens with that store and leaves the argument last. Rebuilt from this note alone and reached the recorded 138 of 138 with ten differing positions on a first build, so the note is complete and reproducible. No improvement this pass. The residual is now pinned as a two-instruction rotation and nothing else: all ten positions hold the same instructions in both builds, with the target opening the snap block with move a2 zero and closing it with li 2 and the store to plus 0x60, and the build doing the exact reverse. Everything between is identical. It is a post-allocation scheduler tie-break between two ready instructions, not a source-shape difference, which is why the six source shapes measured this pass all leave it untouched: storing the 2 through the frame-count local; naming the node x argument in a local; passing the third argument as a zero-valued local rather than a literal; splitting the plus 0x6C read-modify-write into a read, the pair store and a write-back; writing the 2 store first in the block rather than last; and copying the position pair through a local. Four profiles the note had not tried - gcc_2_8_1_g0, gcc_2_8_1_cc_g8_as_g0_split, gcc_2_8_1_g0_no_split and gcc_2_8_1_g0_keep_large_ori - all build 138 and report nine rather than ten, but the rotation is unchanged and the ninth position only aligns by accident because a non-split profile puts the %hi in a different register, so none of them is a reason to move off the module's profile. Also measured: unlike FreeDuel_UpdateCursorTween, the frame count does not need an s16 local here. Writing the decrement, the store and the test directly against the field gives byte-identical code, because the test is a signed relational one that needs sll 16 either way rather than an equality test where the direct form would give andi. The rotation is now half solved and the residual is one instruction rather than two. Declaring the three snap stores volatile does change post-allocation scheduling: the store of 2 into plus 0x60 moves from the top of the block, where the unpinned build puts it, to the end of the block where the target has it, and the whole block shifts into the target's order behind it. So the recorded claim that this is a scheduler tie-break no source shape can reach is too strong; a volatile access is a scheduling barrier and does reach it. The position count stays at ten only because the block shifts by one: what remains is solely the move of zero into a2, the third argument to TextBox_GetGlyphAt, which the target schedules first in the block and both builds schedule last. Pinning only the plus 0x60 store rather than all three leaves the block unchanged, so the barrier has to come before the store that must sink. Correction to the claim I added last pass. Volatile does change post-allocation scheduling here, but it does not reach the target's order and the target's stores are not volatile. The decisive evidence is that the target interleaves a load between two of the three snap stores - lb of D_8016D42C sits between the store of the position pair and the store of 2 into plus 0x60 - and a load cannot cross a volatile store, so those stores cannot be qualified. What pinning actually does is move the plus 0x60 store from the top of the block, where the unqualified build puts it, to the middle; the target has it last. The pinned build is closer in that its first four block instructions match the target's shifted by one, where the unqualified build's do not, but both score ten and the pinned one forbids the interleaving the target shows. So the rotation stands as a scheduler tie-break after all, and the earlier note was right. What the volatile experiment did establish, and what is worth keeping, is that a volatile access is a scheduling barrier as well as a defence against dead store elimination and delay slot motion. Also measured against the pinned shape and not helping: naming the node x argument in a local before the stores, which builds 139, and naming it immediately before the call, which leaves the count and the ten positions unchanged. The residual is the move of zero into a2, which the target places first in the block and every build places last.

name: func_80168CDC
notes: Exact boundary from the verified overlay split. The data-placement blocker recorded here is obsolete: the module_header carve has since happened, and 0x4 to 0x90 is now its own module_rodata subsegment rather than part of module_header. This is an ordinary conversion. This is the password screen's character to tile mapper. It takes a slot index and a widget pointer, indexes D_800EB0F8 with a stride of 100 bytes, reads the Shift-JIS code from the widget and turns it into a u and v pair plus a palette for func_80040510, drawing at the widget's x and y from +0xC and +0xE with a signed shift applied to x. A null widget takes a separate path that draws a fixed 0x80 by 0x80 tile at the coordinates held in the object at D_8016D404. The code path itself is ordinary: a four case switch remapping 0x8171 and 0x8173 to 0x8183 and 0x8172 and 0x8174 to 0x8184, compiled as a balanced comparison tree pivoting on 0x8172; then an unsigned range test for 0x824F to 0x829A which is the fullwidth digits and letters, with the two gaps 0x8259 to 0x825F and 0x827A to 0x8280 rejected, and the cell computed as column of the low nibble times 16 and row of the code minus 0x8240 shifted down and back up by 4 plus 0x48; and otherwise a linear search of a symbol table, where the matched index is itself the position, and a few special cases. The symbol table is a non-static local array with an initialiser, and its exact source form is now measured, not guessed: it is a flat s32 tbl[30], not an array of code/position pairs. Reading the 120 bytes as 4-byte pairs leaves every second halfword zero and splits the terminator, whereas reading them as 30 words gives 29 positive Shift-JIS codes and a final -1, which is what the loop's exit-on-negative test compares against. The function block copies 0x78 bytes from D_80168004 into the frame at sp+0x28 as sixteen byte chunks plus an eight byte tail, then searches the copy with the loop exiting on a negative entry. D_80168004 holds exactly 29 Shift-JIS codes followed by -1, verified word for word against the built module: 0x8149 0x8168 0x8194 0x8190 0x8193 0x8195 0x8166 0x8169 0x816A 0x8196 0x817B 0x8143 0x817C 0x8144 0x815E 0x8146 0x8147 0x8183 0x8181 0x8184 0x8148 0x8140 0x83BF 0x83C0 0x81C1 0x81A9 0x81A8 0x81BC 0x81BD then -1. Those 120 bytes are this function's own initialiser data and they sit at module offset 0x4, immediately after the header word D_80168000, and the yaml already isolates them: module_rodata covers 0x4 to 0x90, so the remaining step is to replace that extracted subsegment with dotted per-source entries and let this C file own 0x4. The source form is verified by probe rather than assumed. Compiling s32 tbl[30] with these 30 word initialisers under gcc_2_8_1_g0_split emits a .rodata section of exactly 0x78 bytes whose contents are byte-identical to module.bin at 0x4, and emits the same block copy as the target at indices 84 to 95: addiu of the end pointer to base+112, four lw, four sw, addiu 16, bne back, then the eight byte tail. Only the register choice differs, which is frame pressure, so the copy shape is not something to chase in the source. First reconstruction, from a standing start to 236 of 240 instructions with 112 differing positions under gcc_2_8_1_g0_split. Six levers were measured rather than guessed. The local array must be declared inside the else block that scans it: declared at function top the 120-byte copy is emitted in the prologue, and only a block-scoped declaration puts it at index 81 where the target has it. The panel struct must be exactly 100 bytes; at 86 the index arithmetic compiles to a different decomposition, and only sizeof 100 reproduces the target's sll 1, addu, sll 3, addu, sll 2. The scan has no pre-test: it compares first and tests the terminator at the bottom with the increment in the delay slot, so it must be written as an unconditional for with an explicit break, and a for (i = 0; tbl[i] >= 0; i++) peels a pre-test that costs instructions. The inner switch has to be on the code and not on tbl[i] even though the two are provably equal there, because only a loop-invariant switch value lets the compiler hoist the three slt comparisons out of the loop into t0, t1 and t2, which is what the target does at 101 to 106; switching on tbl[i] sinks them into the switch and loses four instructions. The fourth and fifth arguments are one variable holding 16, and the sign extension of the shift is written through that same variable as (shift << n) >> n, which is what produces the sllv and srav pair at 190 and 191; written as an (s16) cast the compiler folds it away because the shift is provably small. That variable must be assigned inside each branch after the two calls: assigned at function top it lives across them, takes a callee-saved register, adds an s7 save and restore and grows the frame from 192 to 200. Holding the shift variable that way builds 239 of 240 but with 211 differing positions, so the 236 build is the better base. What is left is four instructions. Rebuilt from this note alone and reached the recorded 236 of 240, so the levers above reproduce. Improved to 237 of 240 with 123 differing positions by one change: the 16 must be a block-scoped declaration with an initialiser, s32 n = 16 as the first statement inside each arm, rather than an assignment to a function-scope local. That is what keeps it in the argument register instead of a shared temporary, and it makes the whole null-widget path byte-exact, li a3 16 then move v0 a3 then sw v0 16(sp) matching the target at 209 to 213. Four placements were measured against this. Assigned once before the if, it also builds 237 but 16 lives in a temporary and is copied in with move a3 t4, and the null path loses its move v0 a3, so the count is the same and the shape is worse. Assigned immediately before the draw call it builds 236 with 180 differing positions. Assigned at function top, before the two calls, it builds 239 but lives across them, takes a callee-saved register, adds an s7 save and restore and grows the frame to 200; that is a genuine trade rather than an improvement. Hoisting the sign-extended shift into its own local before the call is byte-identical to the accepted shape, so that lever is inert and should not be tried again. What is left is three instructions and the main path's arg5 store is the visible one: the target copies the register into v0 and stores the copy before it uses the same register as the shift count, while the build uses it for the shift first and then stores it directly, saving the copy. So the open question is what orders the fifth argument's store ahead of the shift, not how either is written. One position difference that is not a count difference: the build materialises li a3 16 at index 31, at the top of the block, where the target materialises it at 173 just before the call. Now 239 of 240 with 123 differing positions, and the two instructions closed this pass were both semantic rather than cosmetic. The function returns the allocated object. The target's move v0 s4 ahead of the three tail stores is the return value being set up, and the compiler then uses v0 as the base register for those stores instead of the callee-saved register; declared void the build stores through s4 directly and is exactly that instruction short, so the signature is Obj * and not void. The fourth and fifth arguments are also two distinct locals rather than one local passed twice. With a single local the compiler stores the argument register straight into the stack slot and schedules that store after the shift; with two locals the fifth argument's store moves ahead of the shift, which is where the target has it. Measured and worse: spelling both arguments and the shift with plain 16 literals builds 236 because the compiler folds the sign extension away; assigning both locals at the call site instead of at block top builds 237 with 180 differing positions; assigning only the second from the first at the call site builds 238. Measured and inert: s32 m = n and s32 m = 16 at block top are byte-identical, so the second local's initialiser does not matter, only that it is a second local. What is left is one instruction, and the visible residual is the fifth argument's materialisation: the target copies the argument register with move v0 a3 while the build emits li v0 16, and relatedly the build materialises li a3 16 at index 31 at the top of the block where the target materialises it at 173 just before the call. The last instruction is located exactly, by aligning the two instruction streams rather than reading the columns: every other region is length-neutral and the whole difference is one delay slot. At the first gap test the target branches to 171 and fills the slot by duplicating the move s2 zero that sits at 170, the first instruction of the shared not-found tail; the build branches straight to 170 and fills the slot from the fall-through lui v0 0xffff of the second gap test. Both are valid fills of the same branch, and the target's costs one instruction because a duplicate is not free. A false positive worth recording: swapping the two gap tests so the 0x827A range is tested first builds exactly 240 of 240, because then both gap branches duplicate their target's first instruction, but it emits the two range tests in the opposite order from the target and the differing positions rise from 123 to 154. The count is not evidence on its own here. The assignment order inside the arms is load bearing and the recorded order is right: writing gap1's arm as v then u builds 242, writing the not-found tail as v then u builds 244, and doing both builds 241, against 239 for u then v in both. So the open question is narrow: what makes the compiler duplicate the branch target's first instruction into the first gap branch's delay slot while the two range tests stay in the target's order. Calls func_80029528 then allocates through func_800291E0 with 0 and two -1 arguments; writes 0x1E at +0x32 and 0x80 at +0x21; sets flag 0x4 at +0x8 and publishes the pointer to D_8016D4D8. The single lever is that the fields are struct members rather than casts through a byte pointer. Written as *(u16 *)((u8 *)obj + 0x8) the load hoists above the sb at +0x21 which fills the load-delay slot and builds 20 instructions against 21 and also puts the %hi in v1 instead of a0. name: func_8016A080
notes: Exact boundary from the verified overlay split. Builds the password entry screen. It clears the eight bytes at D_8016D410 from the top down and the fields at D_8016D424 and D_8016D428 then calls Password_RefreshDigitDisplay Password_RefreshStarchipDisplay and Password_CreateMessageBox with 226 and 1. It loads the screen background through func_80029574 with D_800EA0E8 keeping it in D_8016D430 and sizing it 320 by 256 and 512 by 240 through the four halfwords at +0x28. It then creates the entry field as a type 2 object at 152 by 40 with widths 2 and 3 depth -8 and flag 0x8 and hands it to func_8016A02C with 1; then a type 1 object at 256 by 120 sized 32 by 32 with 13 in both halfwords at +0x48 whose flag word at +4 loses bit 0x08000000 and gains 0x50000000 before func_80042918 depth 10 hook func_80169E20 and Password_SetDigitCursorTarget - its +0x30 copies its own +0x18 and it is kept in D_8016D420. Finally four type 2 objects are created one per password digit through func_80040468 with 3 1 the index 11 and 524 each gaining bit 0x40000000 depth 8 hook Password_UpdateDigitCursorDecoration and flags 0x28 and stored in D_8016D440; the screen ends with func_8003FF08 of 29520 and func_80015A00. Builds 161 of 161 instructions with 72 differing positions. Lever found: the D_8016D424 and D_8016D428 clears must precede the byte loop not follow it - after the loop the body builds 160 which is one short. Measured and not helping: writing the four background size stores through a local copy of D_8016D430 instead of the global which builds 160; sharing the loop counter with the fourth argument of func_800404CC which also builds 160 even though the target passes a register there rather than zero; an explicit walking pointer for the clear loop which builds 161 with 75 differences; a do-while form; an explicit array size; and pointer syntax for the index. What remains is that the target strength-reduces the clear loop into a walking pointer initialised as base plus 7 and decremented in the branch delay slot while the build recomputes base plus index every iteration. Retested after #787 added a strength-reduce axis: the profile is not suppressing anything. Compiling the clear loop alone with and without -fno-strength-reduce under gcc_2_8_1_g0_split gives byte-identical assembly so the pass is not firing on this loop either way and the reduced form in the target has to come from the source. Probing eight loop spellings directly through the compiler rather than through full overlay builds found it: i equals 7 then p equals the array plus i as its own statement then a for with an empty first clause decrementing both. That reproduces the target exactly including addu of base and the counter register rather than the folded relocation. Writing the pointer as address-of element 7 or as array plus 7 folds the offset into %hi and %lo of symbol plus 7 which the target does not have; indexing the array inside the loop leaves the add inside the loop. With that loop and the four background size stores written through the global the body now builds 161 of 161 with 56 differing positions down from 72. What remains starts at the background pointer: the target stores the func_80029574 result into D_8016D430 in the call's delay slot and then reloads it with lw before the four size stores while every source form tried so far keeps the returned value in a register instead. The background pointer residual is solved: D_8016D430 is volatile. The target stores the func_80029574 result into it in the call's delay slot and then reloads it with lw into a different register before the four size stores, and a probe reproduces that only with the qualifier - plain, through a local copy, and with the global spelled at each store all give byte-identical code that keeps the returned value in a register and never reloads. The probe output matches the target instruction for instruction including which register takes the reload and which takes the constants. This was found by extending tools/project/overlay_scan_reloads.py, which previously could not see this case because it treats any store as a legitimate reason to reload and clears its record. Correction: D_8016D430 is not volatile and the conclusion recorded above is wrong. The reload has an ordinary explanation. The assignment stores D_800EA0E8 into the global and func_80029574 is called after it, so the call invalidates memory and the following read has to reload. The probe that concluded volatile put the store after the call instead of before it, which removed the invalidation and left the qualifier as the only thing that could produce a reload. Worse, volatile is actively wrong here: it stops the store being moved into the call's delay slot, which is where the target has it, so the qualified form spends a nop there. Written unqualified as D_8016D430 = D_800EA0E8 then the call then a local read, the background block matches instruction for instruction. Reconstructed from this note the function now builds 160 of 161 with 73 differing positions and is exact through instruction 90. The one missing instruction is the flag word at plus 4, which the target stores twice, once after clearing bit 0x08000000 and once after setting 0x50000000. Every form tried collapses the two into a single store: two separate compound assignments, an explicit local carrying the value across both, and the two halfword stores at plus 0x48 and plus 0x4A interleaved between them to break up the combination. Now 161 of 161 with nine differing positions, down from the recorded 56, and all nine are register naming rather than instruction differences. Three findings. The flag word at plus 4 is stored twice because the first store is volatile and the second is not. GCC eliminates a first store to the same location in every plain form - seven were measured, including two compound assignments, an explicit local carried across both, recomputing the second value from the original rather than from the first, and interleaving the two halfword stores between them - so something has to defeat dead store elimination. Qualifying both stores does give two stores but costs a nop, because a volatile store cannot be moved into the call's delay slot where the target has the second one. Qualifying only the first gives both effects at once. The general form is worth keeping: use volatile to keep a store that would otherwise be dead, but never on the store that has to fill a delay slot. Second, the loop counter's zero must be assigned just before its first use rather than earlier; assigned early, GCC reuses that register for the unrelated literal zero argument to func_80029574 where the target uses the zero register, which was worth three positions. Third, naming the digit hook Password_UpdateDigitCursorDecoration in a local before the slot pointer rather than spelling it inside the loop swaps s2 and s3 the right way round, worth two more. The remaining nine are the v0 and v1 pairing through the flag block. The remaining nine positions are robust and are a register allocation tie-break rather than a shape. The flag value takes v1 in the build where the target uses v0, and the two constants take the other register, with the instructions otherwise identical. Measured and not helping: reading the flag word before the two halfword stores rather than after; splitting the read from the mask so the read is the first statement of the block; naming the 0x50000000 constant in a local; naming the 13 constant in a local; and qualifying the read volatile as well as the first store. The flag value has much the longer live range and should win the lower register on priority, so whatever decides it is not visible in the source. The nine-position residual reproduces in a twelve-line probe of the flag block alone, which is the most useful thing to record about it: the cluster is intrinsic to that block rather than imported from the rest of the function, so it can be worked at probe cost instead of rebuilding all 161 instructions. The probe shows exactly what decides the pairing. Re-reading the flag word for the second store gives the target's pairing, the value in v0 and the constants in v1, but costs an extra lw, because the volatile first store defeats the common subexpression and forces a real reload. Reusing the masked value from a local gives the target's instruction count and sequence but swaps the pair. Eight reuse spellings were measured and every one is byte-identical: an extra copy local between the two stores, naming the 13 in a local, naming the 0x50000000 in a local, hoisting the read above the two halfword stores, splitting the read from the mask, declaring the value signed, changing declaration order, and moving the halfword stores after the mask. Holding the object in a callee-saved register by taking it from a call, which mirrors the real function where it lives in s0 across two calls, is also inert, so the swap is not an artefact of the probe's simpler context. On the profile axis, gcc_2_8_1_g0_no_sched2_split, gcc_2_8_1_g8_split and gcc_2_8_1_g0_keep_large_ori are identical to the default. gcc_2_8_1_g0_split_no_sched1 does produce the target's v0 and v1 pairing, but it is not the answer: it reorders the block so the mask constant is materialised into v1 before the load rather than into a1, and the target keeps the mask in a1 across the move of the object into a0. So the pairing is now closed against source shape and against the profile knob, and the next idea has to come from somewhere other than this block's spelling.

name: func_8016A37C
notes: Exact boundary from the verified overlay split. Recorded as blocked on data placement in the same way as func_80168CDC, but through a jump table rather than a local array initialiser. That blocker is obsolete: the module_header carve has since happened and 0x4 to 0x90 is now its own module_rodata subsegment. This is the password entry screen's per-frame input handler. It pumps func_80039794, returns early when bit 0x40 of +0x6C of gPassword_pDigitCursorWidget is set or when D_800EB12C masked with 0x2008 is not 0x2000, then takes the low five bits of D_8016D424 as a state, returns if that is 5 or more, and dispatches through jtbl_8016807C. State 0 walks gPassword_nDigitIndex over 0 to 7 on the left and right bits of D_8009B3A4 and plays sound 0x2F through func_8003FEE0; the other four all branch on bits 0x8000 and 0x4000 of the same D_8016D424 word whose low bits chose them, so the upper bits are sub-flags of the state. The blocker is that jtbl_8016807C is compiler-emitted data. Its five words are 0x8016A3FC 0x8016A5C0 0x8016A68C 0x8016A794 and 0x8016A8A0, all inside this function's own body, and they sit at module offset 0x7C to 0x90 inside module_rodata, which now covers 0x4 to 0x90 on its own. The remaining step is to replace that extracted subsegment with dotted per-source entries so this C file owns 0x7C. The three-way split is exact and was read back from module.bin: 0x4 to 0x7C is func_80168CDC's initialiser, 0x7C to 0x90 is these five jump table words, and 0x90 is the SaveLoad string already owned by name_entry_main. Correction to that entry: the two do not have to be converted together. Splat appends undeclared object .rodata after the declared run, so each converted function does have to be declared, but the remainder can stay an extracted blob. Splitting module_rodata into a 0x4 blob and a second blob at 0x7C was built and the password module still hashes to 6925509db80d4ff8869f41350f0256524f5ff15cb9b3bf2f6dc7351a7caf3d55, so whichever function is converted first takes a dotted entry at its own offset and the other keeps a blob at its own. func_80168CDC is therefore convertible on its own. Every unmatched function in all five modules was scanned for jump table references and this is the only one, and the whole overlay set contains exactly one jtbl symbol. Unblocked by the resident match of func_8002D458, which established the .rodata subsegment route for a compiler-emitted jump table, and the route is now verified for this function rather than assumed. A probe of just the guards and the dispatch, compiled with gcc_2_8_1_g0_split, emits a .rodata of exactly 0x14 bytes, five words, which is the size of jtbl_8016807C, and reproduces the target's dispatch instruction for instruction: andi with 0x1f, sltiu against 5, beqz to the default, then sll by 2, addu, lw and jr through the table. The 8-byte alignment the compiler gives that section is not an obstacle: func_8002D458's own table sits at 0x80010224, which is 4 modulo 8, so the generated script places it exactly. Source shapes confirmed by that probe: the state is state = D_8016D424 & 0x1F with a plain switch over cases 0 to 4 and no default body, since the compiler's own range check is what produces the early return; the widget guard is a test of bit 0x40 of +0x6C on D_8016D420; and the second guard must be written as a comparison against 0x2000 rather than as a truth test, because that is what emits li v1 8192 followed by bne. Applying the entry-count lever from func_8002D458: all five table entries are distinct addresses and the bound is 5, so unlike that function there is no hidden case sharing the default block, and the range really is 0 to 4. Case entry points are indices 32, 145, 196, 262 and 329, and the shared return is index 359. Case 0 opens by testing D_8009B3A4 against 0xA000 for left and right, stepping D_8016D428 up with a clamp at 7 or down with a clamp at 0, then playing sound 47 through func_8003FEE0, calling func_8016A00C with the widget, storing 8 into the widget's +0x60 and setting bit 0x40 of its +0x6C; when 0xA000 is clear it falls to a test of D_8009B394 against 0x5000 for up and down at index 71. The remaining yaml work is a single carve: replace the module_rodata blob with a blob covering 0x4 to 0x7C and a dotted entry [0x7C, .rodata, overlays/password/func_8016A37C], leaving name_entry_main's entry at 0x90 alone. The whole function is now decoded and written. All five cases, the dispatch and the shared tail are mapped, and the first full candidate builds 366 instructions against 365, so the structure is close from the start. Four source shapes are established by measurement. The three pad globals must be declared the way main_menu already declares them, extern volatile u16 X[] read through index 0: the target reads each of D_8009B3A4, D_8009B394 and D_8009B398 twice, and without volatile the compiler folds each pair into one load, which is structurally wrong even though it is shorter. Adding volatile moved the first divergence from index 34 to index 130. The result of func_8016A304 must be assigned straight into D_8016D4DC rather than through a local, because a local costs a move before the store. func_80021894 takes D_8016D4DC as an argument rather than none; that single correction took the differing positions from 358 to 145, which is the largest single improvement found for this function and is why the argument list is worth reading off the delay slots rather than assumed. Case 1 falls through into case 2 with no break, ending with a store of 2 into D_8016D424 and continuing into case 2's body. Case 3 steps a counter down by a cascade whose divisors are 10, 20, 30 and 40 under guards of 10, 100, 1000 and 10000, with a final step of 1 when the division yields zero. Best measured state is 374 instructions with 145 differing positions. Measured and worse: hoisting the D_8016D424 = w & 0xBFFF store above the D_8009B34D test, which the target appears to do through a delay slot, costs an instruction and is not the right reading. Now 365 of 365 instructions with 37 differing positions, all of them in one cluster. Four further levers, each measured. The counter at D_8016D438 is unsigned: the target's cascade uses multu and sltiu, so declaring it and the step u32 rather than s32 removes the signed-division bias idiom and took the build from 372 to 364 instructions, eight fewer. D_801D07E0 must be declared as an element of an array based at 0x801D0000, index 504, not as a scalar; that is the same declared-size lever func_8002D458 recorded, and it is what produces the split lui and addiu base that both the load and the store at 2016 then share. It closed the last instruction and took the differing positions from 99 to 55. The f21 byte of D_8016D4D8 is read unsigned in case 1, where the target uses lbu against zero, and signed in case 4, where it uses lb against zero, so the member is u8 with an s8 cast at the case 4 test. And the state word needs its own local in each case rather than one shared local across all four; sharing it merges the live ranges and misallocates the pair, and splitting them took 54 differing positions to 37. Correction to the earlier entry: hoisting the D_8016D424 = w & 0xBFFF store above the D_8009B34D test is right after all. It was measured as worse only against the candidate that still had func_80021894 taking no argument; on the corrected base it takes 374 with 145 to 372 with 125, which agrees with the target putting that store in the branch delay slot. Measured and inert: dropping case 3's state local and testing D_8016D424 directly. What is left is a uniform register shift through case 3's step cascade, where the target holds the counter in a0, the step in the callee-saved s0 and the mfhi temporary in a3, and the build holds them in a1, a0 and t0. Down to five differing positions at 365 of 365, and the register cluster recorded last pass was two separate variable-identity problems rather than a scheduling artefact. The first is the pattern already recorded elsewhere in this module: case 0's digit and case 3's step are the same source local, not two. The target holds both in s0, and merging them so the cascade assigns into the same variable that case 0 uses for the scanned digit took the differing positions from 37 to 8 on its own, with the whole cascade's register shift disappearing at once. The second is that case 3 needs its own local for the card id: writing D_8016D438 = D_801A8000[D_8016D4DC].lo directly costs three positions, and reading D_8016D4DC into a local first took 8 to 5. Measured and inert against that: declaring the step signed, hoisting the pool read-modify-write into an explicit temporary either side of the counter update, spelling it as an explicit self-referencing store, taking a pointer to the pool slot, and declaring the pool array's element type signed. Measured and much worse: loading the pool before the cascade rather than after, which builds 45 differing positions, and declaring the counter and D_8016D438 signed again, which returns to 373 instructions and confirms the unsigned reading is load bearing. What is left is a single v0 against v1 swap on the pool's read-modify-write, where the target keeps the 0x801D0000 base in v0 and the loaded value in v1 and the build has them the other way round; no source spelling tried so far moves it.

name: NameEntry_BuildStarterDeck
notes: Exact overlay match with gcc_2_8_1_g0_split. Weighted random draw over the card pools. It clears a 722-byte local tally then walks the null-terminated table of pool pointers at D_8016D3DC; each pool begins with a u16 draw count followed by one u16 weight per card. For each draw it takes a threshold of func_8008E590 masked to 0x7FF plus one and accumulates weights until the running total reaches it. The selected index is kept only while its tally is below 3: the tally is bumped, index plus one is appended to the s16 list at D_801D0200 and func_8002CCE4 is called with index plus 289; otherwise the draw count is incremented so the draw is retried. Three levers: the tally test is written as index greater than or equal to 3 with the retry as the then-arm so the keep-arm is the else and is laid out after it; the list pointer advances after the call rather than before; and the threshold is computed as the first statement of the draw body which is what puts the pool pointer in s4 and the threshold in s5 rather than the other way round. That last one is pure register allocation and was the whole residual at 79 of 79 instructions with 9 differing positions.

name: NameEntry_Main
notes: Exact overlay match with gcc_2_8_1_g0_split. Clears the 0x3000 buffer at D_801D0000 and decompresses D_80168090 into it; polls func_80012D4C and func_8008E590 until NameEntry_PollCompletion reports ready; then XORs the twelve bytes at D_801D0200 + 0x40C and combines them with D_8009B09C shifted left by 8 to seed the word at D_801D0200 + 0x334; retrying with func_8008E590 while the seed is zero. D_801D0200 needs a base local or the 0x40C folds into the relocation. The retry loop stores inside its own condition which is what puts the call block before the test.
